title: Shiny on the outside
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever polished something up to look better than it really was? a story, a photo, a reason?
options: me too. then this one is for us. listen.
then you’ll spot the trick in this one. listen.

steps.line: On one of his journeys, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana stopped at a roadside inn run by a man named Sajjan.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: Sajjan seemed so holy. He had built a temple for his Hindu guests and a mosque for his Muslim guests, and welcomed every traveler.
But at night, while his guests slept, Sajjan robbed them. His holiness was a mask.

steps.q: Why would a robber build a temple and a mosque for his guests?
o: To ease his conscience about the robbing
So travelers of every faith would trust him
To earn praise from the local ruler
steps.why: A temple and a mosque made every traveler feel safe. Even his name, Sajjan, means a good man, a friend.

steps.q: That night Guru Nanak stays awake. What do you think he does?
o: Asks Mardana to play, and sings
steps.why: No guards and no running. He trusted one true song to reach Sajjan’s heart.

steps.line: That night, Guru Nanak asked Mardana to play, and he sang. Sajjan, waiting in the dark, stopped to listen.
The song said: bronze is bright and shiny, but rub it, and its blackness shows. Wash it a hundred times, and it still won’t come clean.

steps.q: Sajjan stands in the dark and hears the song about the bronze. What do you think he does?
o: Falls at the Guru’s feet and confesses
Slips off into the night with his loot
Waits for the singing to stop, then robs them
steps.why: He knew the song was about him. He confessed, gave away what he’d stolen, and, many tellings say, turned his inn into a dharamsal, an early Sikh gathering place.

steps.line: Sajjan knew the song was about him. He fell at the Guru’s feet, told the truth, and gave what he had stolen to the poor.
At the top of the Sikh scripture, God is called Sat Naam: truth is the name. Sat means what really is, not what shines.
steps.label: today

steps.q: In the song, the bronze shines until it’s rubbed. What does the rubbing stand for?
o: A close look at how you live
steps.why: Shine is easy; rubbing tests it. A holy look can’t survive a close look at what you do in the dark.

say: here’s what i love. the guru didn’t shout or call the guards. he sang one true song, and the mask came off by itself.
sikhs call god sat naam, truth is the name, and karta purakh, the creator. so when you stop pretending and tell the truth, in a way you’re saying that name.

steps.q: Sat means “what really is.” Before Sajjan changed, what was really true about him?
o: The holy places he built for guests
What he did when no one was looking
The welcome he gave at the door
steps.why: Sat is what’s really there, not what shines. His truth was what he did in the dark, until he told it and changed.

today.say: today, say one true thing you’ve been polishing over. small is fine: “sorry, that was me,” or “honestly, i’m not okay.”
options: then say it today. truth is the name.
then just catch one little shine today, and let it go.

tomorrow.title: The boulder on the hill.
tomorrow.line: a thirsty friend, a proud holy man, and one raised hand.

card.keepWhy: Shiny isn’t the same as true.
sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak and Sajjan (often called Sajjan Thag), near Tulamba, with Mardana
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Suhi, Mahalla 1 (“ujal kaiha chilkana, ghotim kaalri mas…”: bronze is bright and shiny, but rubbed, its blackness shows; washed a hundred times, its impurity stays)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar: Sat Naam, Karta Purakh)
check: In most tellings Sajjan murdered as well as robbed his guests; the lesson softens this to “robbed”.
Confirm “gave what he had stolen to the poor” (tellings say he gave his wealth to the poor and his inn became a place of worship).
